post-13261.title: Housing and San Juan County’s Comprehensive Plan Update
post-13261.summary: Friends explains why housing belongs in San Juan County's Comprehensive Plan: nearly half of homes sit vacant, rents outpace wages, and sprawl fragments forests and farmland. post-12280.title: Friends of the San Juans Restores Critical Shoreline Habitat at Neck Point, Shaw Island
post-12280.summary: At Neck Point on Shaw Island, crews remove rockfall and old bulkhead remnants that buried a surf smelt and sand lance spawning beach, then nourish 500 feet of shoreline with sand and gravel. Natural sediment now moves again, feeding forage fish, salmon, seabirds and orcas while still protecting the road.

image.caption: Shoreline at Neck Point on Shaw Island

images.caption: Shoreline at Neck Point on Shaw Island

Move the arrow to see before (left photo) and after (right photo) at Neck Point on Shaw Island. Crews removed excess armoring rock that had been burying forage fish spawning habitat and disrupting natural beach processes. Notice the shift from angular quarry rock and boulders to natural mixed sand and gravel substrate—the grain sizes that surf smelt and Pacific sand lance need for successful egg deposition. Today, the east end of the shoreline is fully restored, reconnecting sediment transport, supporting forage fish and salmon, and nourishing the beach in front of the road to protect infrastructure while sustaining habitat.

post-12280.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans completed a major shoreline restoration at Neck Point on Shaw Island, removing excess rock and bulkhead remnants to restore natural beach processes and critical spawning habitat for forage fish. post-11775.title: Community Rallies to Protect San Juan Shorelines from Invasive Green Crab
post-11775.summary: State biologists confirm eight invasive European green crabs at False Bay on San Juan Island, the county's first detection since 2019. post-12276.title: Student advocacy pays off: Recycling Reform Act signed into law!
post-12276.summary: Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students travel to Olympia and help pass Washington's Recycling Reform Act, which makes producers pay for packaging waste and expands curbside recycling. post-11385.title: A simple solution to pollution!

post-11310.title: New Boating Rules Now in Effect Protecting Southern Resident Killer Whales
post-11310.summary: Since January 2025, Washington boaters must stay 1,000 yards from Southern Resident killer whales, slow to 7 knots within that zone, and stop if a whale comes within 400 yards. Friends helped pass these rules because engine noise masks the echolocation orcas use to hunt scarce Chinook salmon.

image.caption: southern resident orcas in the ocean

images.caption: southern resident orcas in the ocean

post-11310.excerpt: New boating rules are now in effect to protect endangered Southern Resident killer whales in Washington waters. Effective January 1, 2025, boaters must stay at least 1,000 yards away from Southern Residents, slow or stop within 400 yards, and reduce vessel noise to lessen disturbance. Friends of the San Juans helped champion these protections to reduce stress and improve the orcas’ ability to forage and thrive in the Salish Sea.

post-11294.title: Ban Discontinued Dispersants and Update Oil Spill Response Plans
post-11294.summary: Stockpiles of discontinued chemical dispersants are still approved for oil spill response in Washington waters, even though they break oil into droplets that increase exposure for marine life and people. Friends asks decision-makers to ban them and add citizen advisory councils to spill planning.

image.caption: yellow plane releasing chemicals while flying over land

images.caption: yellow plane releasing chemicals while flying over land

post-11294.excerpt: Did you know the chemicals used to clean up oil spills can be as harmful as the spills themselves? Stockpiles of discontinued chemical dispersants with known health risks are still approved for use in Washington waters. These toxic dispersants threaten marine life, human health, and shoreline communities near the Salish Sea. Friends of the San Juans is calling on state and federal decision‑makers to remove discontinued dispersants from oil spill response plans, update planning to prioritize safety and transparency, and establish citizen oversight councils to protect people and ecosystems.

post-10695.title: Summer Tide Pool School

post-10679.summary: Representative Rick Larsen meets Friends on San Juan Island and voices support for continued federal funding of eelgrass mapping and other shoreline restoration through the EPA, NOAA and Fish and Wildlife. post-10465.title: Become a Green Boater Today!
post-10465.summary: Friends' Green Boater pledge asks boaters to anchor beyond eelgrass, give whales space and leave a clean wake. Herring spawn on eelgrass in only a few county bays, including Eastsound, West Sound, Blind Bay, Mud Bay and Hunter Bay, so dropping anchor deeper than 25 feet protects the food web that feeds salmon and orcas.

post-10463.title: Diving into eelgrass health
post-10463.summary: Friends, DNR, and Friday Harbor Labs are mapping eelgrass in 21 bays and comparing it to a 2003 survey; last summer showed declines in 12 bays, mostly in shallow water. Eelgrass shelters forage fish and young Chinook, so knowing where it thrives guides protection for salmon and orcas.

post-10285.title: Artists on Yellow Island
post-10285.summary: Nearly forty artists and a Lummi council member join Friends' first Artist Expedition to Yellow Island in April, sketching camas, chocolate lily and shooting star in bloom. post-6828.summary: Ken Carrasco, a retired marine biologist on Orcas Island, serves as president of Friends' board. His Coast Guard icebreaker service and two years researching the Exxon Valdez spill shaped his conviction about climate change and clean, quiet boating on the Salish Sea.

post-10095.title: Action Update: Who foots the bill for an oil spill?
post-10095.summary: Friends' outreach on Washington's oil-facility financial responsibility rule generates more than 200 public comments, a 27-organization letter, and a Seattle Times op-ed. The rule decides whether refineries and pipelines, not taxpayers, cover the full cost of a major spill.

Learn how to submit comments and advocate for stronger financial responsibility requirements to protect the Salish Sea.

post-10103.title: Action Update: Phillips 66
post-10103.summary: After an anonymous tip about unpermitted changes at the Phillips 66 refinery in Ferndale, Friends pushes Whatcom County for review, comments and appeals until a February 2024 settlement. post-10038.title: Shoreline Property Owner Workshop Recording + Tools
post-10038.summary: More than 90 percent of waterfront parcels in the San Juans are private homes, so landowners hold the key to healthy shorelines. post-9990.title: Business and Organizations that Show Up for Friends!

post-9116.title: Current Volunteer Opportunities

post-9717.summary: Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students lobby District 40 legislators in Olympia for the Re-Wrap Act, which makes producers pay for packaging waste. post-9595.title: Unit 3: The loss of the Sunflower Star
post-9595.summary: Sunflower sea stars, which grow up to 24 arms and once anchored the Salish Sea food web, lost nearly 90 percent of their population to wasting disease after 2012. This 360-degree video visits Jason Hodin's lab at Friday Harbor Laboratories, where scientists are raising the stars to rebuild the population.

image.caption: sunflower sea star

Once one of the fastest and largest sea stars in the world—and a crucial part of the Salish Sea ecosystem—the species declined by nearly 90% after sea star wasting disease. Scientists are now racing to rebuild their population and restore balance to the marine environment.

post-9527.title: Legislative Action Alerts!

post-9492.title: Take a stand against big oil in support of the Salish Sea!

post-9492.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans calls on community members to take a stand against fossil fuel expansion and support protections for the Salish Sea. By submitting public comments, individuals can help address risks from increased vessel traffic, pollution, and threats to marine life.

images.caption: map pinpointing broken point on shaw island

post-9417.excerpt: Discover how Friends of the San Juans and partners removed a toxic bulkhead on Shaw Island and restored a natural beach that supports forage fish, salmon, and vital shoreline habitat in the Salish Sea.

post-9459.title: Unit 1: Explore the Marine Food Web
post-9459.summary: This classroom unit uses 360-degree underwater video of herring and salmon habitat to show how Salish Sea shorelines feed forage fish, salmon, and orcas. Slides, a food web activity, and discussion questions help students see why healthy beaches and kelp beds matter.

images.caption: herring bull kelp

post-9459.excerpt: Discover how the shorelines of the Salish Sea support forage fish, salmon, and orcas. Swim through kelp beds and follow migrating salmon to explore the biodiverse marine food web — from tiny invertebrates to mighty whales — in this immersive educational unit.

post-9512.title: Unit 2: Mighty Herring
post-9512.summary: Pacific herring are small schooling fish that feed salmon, seabirds, seals, and ultimately Southern Resident orcas, and hold deep cultural and economic value. image.caption: school of herring

images.caption: school of herring

post-9512.excerpt: Pacific herring may be small fish — but in the Salish Sea, they play a huge role. In this unit, you’ll learn how these “mighty” forage fish support salmon and orcas, nourish entire marine food webs, and bring shorelines to life when they spawn. Through 360° video, follow scientists and community-science volunteers as they document herring spawning underneath the waters of the San Juan Islands.

post-9273.title: Friends’ Action Ensures Refinery Project Will Not Impact endangered Orca
post-9273.summary: Friends appeals a Whatcom County permit for a Phillips 66 refinery pipe bridge whose purpose, including possible oil transfers at the dock, was unclear. The settlement limits the pipes to propane and butane, keeps them off the dock and allows inspections, so no new tanker traffic threatens Southern Resident orcas.

images.caption: phillips 66 ferndale refinery at night

post-9273.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans took action to ensure a refinery project would not increase vessel traffic in the Salish Sea, securing protections for endangered Southern Resident killer whales and their critical habitat through enforceable conditions and oversight.

post-9269.title: Fall into Great Islands Clean Up
post-9269.summary: The Fall Great Islands Clean Up on September 30, 2023 gathers volunteers at Jackson Beach, Eastsound Village Green, Lopez Village Park and Shaw's ballfield to clear litter from roads and beaches. image.caption: orange and yellow flowers

images.caption: orange and yellow flowers

post-8852.title: Reject Roberts Bank Terminal 2!
post-8852.summary: Friends urges rejection of Roberts Bank Terminal 2, a new over-water shipping terminal the size of 202 football fields in the Fraser River estuary. post-8775.excerpt: A major victory for Southern Resident killer whales as new protections are secured to reduce vessel disturbance and improve the chances of recovery for this endangered population in the Salish Sea. The decision marks an important step forward in long-term conservation efforts.

post-8771.title: Movie Night! Right-sizing the fight for the Right Whale
post-8771.summary: Friends and the San Juan Island Yacht Club host a free May 2023 screening of Right Over the Edge, a film following scientists searching for the North Pacific right whale, of which about thirty remain. Filmmaker Kevin Campion answers questions after showings in Friday Harbor and at Eastsound's SeaView Theatre.

image.caption: the north pacific right whale

images.caption: the north pacific right whale

post-8771.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans hosts a community movie night at the Yacht Club, bringing people together for an evening of film, conversation, and connection centered around shared care for the Salish Sea and local environment.

post-8766.title: Green Crab Community Science Opportunity
post-8766.summary: Invasive European green crab, first found locally at Westcott Bay in 2016, threatens shellfish, young Dungeness crab, and the eelgrass beds that shelter juvenile salmon. Friends coordinates volunteer molt surveys for San Juan County, with training workshops on Lopez and Orcas so beachgoers can spot early signs.

image.caption: person holding a large european green crab

images.caption: person holding a large european green crab

post-8766.excerpt: Calling all community scientists, volunteers, shoreline landowners, and beachgoers! The invasive European green crab threatens eelgrass, shellfish, juvenile salmon, and our marine ecosystem. We need you — help monitor beaches by joining our 20-minute green-crab molt surveys. Friends of the San Juans is coordinating this effort across San Juan County.

post-8764.title: Inspiration & Friendship
post-8764.summary: Board member Janet Alderton remembers her friend Irmgard Conley of Olga on Orcas Island, whose commitment to keeping the San Juans green once included selling property to sustain Friends. Her legacy continues through the Irmgard Conley Islands Conservation Fund.

image.caption: sailboat at sunset

images.caption: sailboat at sunset

post-8764.excerpt: A reflection on the power of friendship, connection, and shared commitment to protecting the San Juan Islands and the Salish Sea, honoring the relationships and community ties that inspire lasting environmental stewardship.

post-8761.title: Crashing into CARA: How I met Irmgard Conley
post-8761.summary: Krystyna Wolniakowski remembers Irmgard Conley, an Orcas Island sailor and Friends board member who died at 94 in January 2023, from a storm-tossed collision in East Sound in 1980 to decades of friendship in Olga. Irmgard's tenacity for salmon, ecosystems and political action shaped how her friends work to protect the islands.

image.caption: sailboat at sunset

images.caption: sailboat at sunset

post-8761.excerpt: A personal reflection on how Irmgard Conley’s story and friendship shaped a meaningful connection, honoring shared experiences, community ties, and the impact of individual lives woven into the fabric of the San Juan Islands.

post-8696.title: Introducing Eva Schulte, Executive Director!
post-8696.summary: Friends' board appoints Eva Schulte as Executive Director in spring 2023, bringing leadership from the Whatcom Community College Foundation, the Sierra Club Foundation and impact investing with American Indian communities. Member support funds eelgrass surveys, safer shipping advocacy, shoreline restoration for salmon and youth climate education.

image.caption: group of people holding hands during a sunset picture as they face the ocean

images.caption: group of people holding hands during a sunset picture as they face the ocean

post-8696.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans welcomes Eva Schulte as Executive Director. With extensive leadership experience in the social and environmental sectors, Eva brings a strong commitment to protecting the Salish Sea and advancing the organization’s mission.

post-8642.title: Welcoming three new board members!
post-8642.summary: Friends welcomes board members Erin Licata of the Samish Indian Nation, Jan Knudson, and Joseph Cohen of Orcas Island, and thanks departing members. Jan joined after touring Friends' Sucia Island restoration project.

image.caption: aerial image of the san juan islands by jess newley

images.caption: aerial image of the san juan islands by jess newley

post-8642.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans welcomes three new board members who bring diverse experience in environmental advocacy, science, and community leadership to support the organization’s mission of protecting the Salish Sea.

post-8640.title: Friends’ litigation to protect the Salish Sea
post-8640.summary: Friends' lawsuit over the Army Corps of Engineers' decision on the BP Cherry Point terminal draws regional news coverage. The groups argue the Corps' vessel limit is no real limit and undermines Magnuson-era protections against oil tanker traffic in the Salish Sea.

image.caption: Photo by Chris LeBoutillier on Unsplash

images.caption: Photo by Chris LeBoutillier on Unsplash

post-8640.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans is taking legal action to protect the Salish Sea, holding decision-makers accountable and defending critical environmental protections for marine life, shorelines, and communities that depend on a healthy ecosystem.

post-8627.title: Friday Harbor Youth Storm the Capitol!
post-8627.summary: Six Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students spend a day in Olympia with Friends' Jess Newley, meeting Representative Alex Ramel, touring the House floor and watching bills like the WRAP Act move through committee. Students share their climate concerns and learn how island voices reach the legislature.

image.caption: Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students at the Washington State Capitol

images.caption: Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students at the Washington State Capitol

post-8627.excerpt: Friday Harbor High School Eco Club students traveled to Olympia for a firsthand look at the legislative process, meeting with lawmakers and advocating for environmental issues impacting island communities. The experience empowered youth to engage in policy and speak up for the future of the Salish Sea.

post-8555.title: King Tides or Plastic Tides?
post-8555.summary: King tides push plastic and styrofoam high onto island beaches, including a six-foot styrofoam cube pulled off Low Island and styrofoam tires washing up on Yellow Island and near Point Caution. Friends asks islanders to adopt a beach and clean up debris before it spreads, and county waste sites take beach trash free.

image.caption: two staff members in orange work jackets carry buckets on the shoreline

images.caption: two staff members in orange work jackets carry buckets on the shoreline

post-8555.excerpt: The creatures that call these islands home need your help! If you enjoyed a stroll on the beach after the last set of king tides, you might have noticed an influx of debris and trash. During extreme high tide events, plastic waste and styrofoam float to the surface and are carried up further onto the […]

post-8533.title: Take Action—Ecology Needs to Hear from You!
post-8533.summary: Washington Ecology proposes updated oil transfer rules with seismic protection and tank decommissioning requirements, but leaves a loophole exempting transfers under 500 gallons per minute from pre-booming. Friends asks islanders to comment by March 5 so spills are contained before they reach orcas and salmon.
post-8533.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans is calling on community members to speak up for environmental protections in the Salish Sea. Learn what’s at stake and how you can take simple, effective action to make your voice heard and help protect local ecosystems.

post-8152.title: Understanding Ecology’s rulemaking to reduce oil spill risks and impacts
post-8152.summary: Washington moves 10 billion gallons of oil through 12,000 transfers a year, and Ecology's rule update leaves gaps: no seismic standards for older containment and no pre-booming for transfers under 500 gallons per minute. Near Vendovi Island, un-boomed anchorage transfers jump from two in 2014 to 76 in 2021.

image.caption: oil slick

images.caption: oil slick

post-8152.excerpt: Washington’s Department of Ecology is proposing updates to oil handling and vessel transfer rules aimed at strengthening spill prevention and protecting the Salish Sea from oil transport risks.

post-13922.title: Important Lessons Learned From an Oil Spill
post-13922.summary: In September 2022 crews raise the fishing vessel Aleutian Isle from 200 feet off the west side of San Juan Island and remove its remaining fuel. Friends' lessons: stage spill gear and crews in the county, fund orca deterrence boats year-round, and have air monitors ready near San Juan County Park.

image.caption: Image: USCG Sector Puget Sound

images.caption: Image: USCG Sector Puget Sound

post-13922.excerpt: The sinking of the fishing vessel Aleutian Isle and resulting oil spill near San Juan Island revealed critical gaps in oil spill response capacity. Friends of the San Juans outlines key lessons learned and actions needed to better protect the Salish Sea from future spills.

post-7438.title: Legal Victory for Friends of the San Juans against Phillips 66 Refinery’s proposal to construct new storage tanks
post-7438.summary: The Washington Court of Appeals rules for Friends in its challenge to Phillips 66's new crude and fuel oil storage tanks at its Ferndale refinery. Because the refinery never quantified added tanker traffic, permit conditions now require annual vessel monitoring so the project does not increase shipping impacts on Southern Resident killer whales.

image.caption: factories of phillips 66 with the smoke stacks

images.caption: factories of phillips 66 with the smoke stacks

post-7438.excerpt: Read how Friends of the San Juans successfully challenged Phillips 66’s proposed storage tank project in court, securing stronger conditions to prevent increased vessel traffic and protect the Salish Sea and Southern Resident killer whales.

post-12036.title: West Sound Beach Restoration (Orcas)
post-12036.summary: On Orcas Island's West Sound, a priority forage fish spawning region, landowners moved their house back from the shore so Friends could remove a rock and creosote bulkhead in 2015. Crews hauled out 530 tons of rock and fill, planted 1,600 native trees and shrubs, and restored 150 feet of pocket beach.

image.caption: family tides farm pre-project

family tides farm post-project

post-12036.excerpt: The West Sound Beach project restored 150 feet of pocket beach on Orcas Island by removing a creosote bulkhead, over 530 tons of rock and fill, and replanting 1,600 native trees and shrubs. The restoration enhanced forage fish spawning, juvenile salmon habitat, and reconnected sediment, beach, and riparian areas for a healthier coastal ecosystem.

post-12034.title: Turn Point Marsh and Beach Restoration (San Juan)
post-12034.summary: At Turn Point on San Juan Island, Friends removes 60 cubic yards of unnecessary rock bulkhead from 200 feet of shoreline in 2009, reconnecting a rare salt marsh to the sea. Sand and gravel nourishment restores spawning beach for surf smelt and sand lance and opens habitat for juvenile salmon.

Turn Point Marsh after restoration

post-12034.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans is working to restore Turn Point Marsh and adjacent beach habitat on San Juan Island, improving shoreline resilience, enhancing habitat for fish and wildlife, and supporting the long-term health of coastal ecosystems.

post-12033.title: Thatcher Bay Nearshore Restoration (Blakely)
post-12033.summary: In 2013 Friends and Blakely Island Timberlands remove a log-handling facility, 955 cubic yards of concrete and fill, and over 20 creosote pilings from northern Thatcher Bay, restoring 200 feet of surf smelt spawning beach. A smaller rebuilt barge landing keeps forest access while uncovering 5,000 square feet of intertidal habitat for juvenile Chinook.

The restoration enhanced forage fish spawning, juvenile salmon habitat, and coastal ecosystem health while maintaining minimal access for forest stewardship.

post-12032.title: Smuggler’s Cove Road Forage Fish Spawning Habitat Enhancement (Shaw)
post-12032.summary: On Blind Bay, Shaw Island, Friends and San Juan County Public Works shrink the rock footprint protecting Smuggler's Cove Road, pull large rock off the beach and add sand and gravel along 300 feet of a surf smelt spawning beach in 2009. Road armoring is the county's biggest threat to forage fish spawning habitat.

post-12032.excerpt: On Shaw Island’s Blind Bay, the Smuggler’s Cove Road project enhanced a known forage fish spawning beach by removing unnatural rocks, reducing road impacts, and adding sand and gravel. The project improved habitat conditions, raised awareness of healthy beach ecosystems, and supported marine food webs.

post-12031.title: Shoal Bay Tide Channel & Lagoon Restoration (Lopez)
post-12031.summary: In 2009 Friends removed a derelict concrete tide gate and 20 truckloads of fill from the channel of Shoal Bay lagoon on Lopez Island. Water now flows freely, summer temperatures drop, and schools of young salmon appear in the five-acre lagoon within months, alongside herring, surf smelt, and shellfish beds.

post-12031.excerpt: The Shoal Bay restoration removed a derelict tide gate and excess fill to restore a five-acre lagoon on Lopez Island. The project improved water quality, fish passage, and habitat for juvenile salmon, forage fish, and local shellfish, with volunteers helping to replant marsh and dune vegetation.

post-12030.title: Salmon Point Forage Fish Spawn Habitat Restoration (Lopez)
post-12030.summary: At Salmon Point on the south end of Lopez Island, Friends and the local community remove 42 cubic yards of failed rock armor and four creosote logs from a surf smelt spawning beach in 2021. With 220 native trees and shrubs planted along 430 feet of shore, forage fish and juvenile salmon gain habitat.

post-12029.title: Neck Point Wetland Restoration (Shaw)
post-12029.summary: Friends removes a 55-cubic-yard berm that blocked tidal flow into the Neck Point salt marsh on Shaw Island, restoring channels so high tides flood the marsh and low tides flush it. Salt marshes supply insect prey for juvenile salmon, and fish are now seen using the reopened channels.

post-12026.title: Mud Bay Wetland and Beach Restoration (Sucia)
post-12026.summary: At Mud Bay on Sucia Island, Friends and Washington State Parks remove nearly 300 feet of low road, fill, rock armor and an undersized culvert in 2020, letting the tide reach the salt marsh for the first time in 75 years. The restored beach and marsh feed young Chinook migrating past Sucia.

post-12024.title: Fisherman Bay Marsh and Beach Restoration (Lopez)
post-12024.summary: Friends, the Land Bank, and private landowners remove old rock and wood ditches, dikes, and berms along 400 feet of salt marsh at Fisherman Bay on Lopez in 2017. Tidal water, nutrients, and juvenile fish now move freely between marsh and bay, and 50 native shrubs replace a mowed edge.

post-12022.title: Broken Point Beach Habitat Restoration (Shaw)
post-12022.summary: At Broken Point on Shaw Island, a landowner partners with Friends to remove a 235-foot creosote wood bulkhead, completed in 2023. The removal uncovers about 4,400 square feet of upper beach and 5,000 square feet of backshore, which are replanted with native vegetation so natural shoreline processes can return.

post-12021.title: Blind Bay Forage Fish Spawn Habitat Restoration (Shaw)
post-12021.summary: In 2017 and 2019 Friends and landowners along Blind Bay on Shaw Island remove about 120 cubic yards of armor rock that buried the beach and add sand and gravel fish mix. post-12018.summary: On Brown Island's southeast shore near Friday Harbor, Friends and three private landowners remove rock armor from a feeder bluff and upper beach, restoring sediment supply, uncovering possible forage fish spawning habitat and letting shoreline vegetation spread. Small parcels, multiple owners and unneeded rock make it a typical island shoreline.

post-12025.summary: On the spit at Shoal Bay, Lopez Island, an old concrete shuffleboard court and creosote bulkhead covered 65 feet of documented surf smelt spawning beach. post-13211.title: Buoy Upgrade Program
post-13211.summary: Herring in San Juan County spawn only in a few eelgrass bays, including West Sound, Blind Bay, Garrison Bay, Mud Bay, and Shoal Bay, and their numbers are critically depressed. Friends offers waterfront owners funding and technical help to upgrade or relocate mooring buoys and remove debris so eelgrass and herring can recover.

images.caption: school of herring

post-13211.excerpt: Attention island residents located near herring spawning grounds!  Pacific herring – also known as forage fish – play a key role in marine food webs as food for out-migrating juvenile salmon, seabirds, and even marine mammals. Herring rely on sensitive eelgrass meadows found along our tidelands to spawn and incubate their eggs. Herring spawning populations […]

post-13989.title: BREAKING: Xylene Manufacture and Export in Anacortes Stopped!
post-13989.summary: Marathon Petroleum withdraws plans to make and export 15,000 barrels a day of xylene from its Anacortes refinery, after Friends and five partner groups appeal the permits and reach a settlement. The Salish Sea avoids 120 added tank vessel transits, with their noise and spill risk for Southern Resident orcas.
post-13989.excerpt: A major victory for the Salish Sea: plans to manufacture and export toxic xylene from the Anacortes refinery were withdrawn after years of community advocacy and legal action. The decision prevents increased tanker traffic and reduces risks to orcas, marine ecosystems, and shoreline communities.

post-13992.title: Action Alert: Require Whatcom County to Address Philips 66 Project’s Impacts to the Southern Resident Orcas
post-13992.summary: Whatcom County issues a mitigated determination for Phillips 66's new 300,000-barrel crude and 80,000-barrel fuel oil tanks at Ferndale without addressing added tanker traffic, oil spill risk or the Southern Resident killer whales whose critical habitat borders the terminal. Friends asks people to comment by August 2, 2019.

post-13998.title: You did it! All Orca Emergency Response Bills Passed!
post-13998.summary: In 2019 the Washington Legislature passes all five Orca Emergency Response bills, covering oil transportation safety, vessel distance from Southern Residents, whale watching guidelines, toxic pollution, and Chinook abundance. Friends, which co-petitioned for the whales' federal listing in 2001, thanks islanders who contacted their representatives.

image.caption: legislation room showing desks with orca hats on the chairs

images.caption: legislation room showing desks with orca hats on the chairs

post-13998.excerpt: A package of Washington State bills aimed at protecting endangered Southern Resident killer whales has passed the legislature. These measures address key threats—including vessel disturbance and habitat impacts—to support orca recovery in the Salish Sea.

post-13994.title: Watch the Video: 3/20 Protect What You Love Orca Event
post-13994.summary: At a March 2019 event in Friday Harbor, Friends and orca researcher Dr. Deborah Giles explain what Southern Resident orcas need to survive, from Chinook salmon to healthy county shorelines. The recording shows how islanders can press elected officials for orca protection and recovery.

image.caption: orca jumping out of the ocean

images.caption: orca jumping out of the ocean

post-13994.excerpt: The Protect What You Love campaign highlights simple actions people can take to safeguard the San Juan Islands and Salish Sea—from protecting marine habitats to supporting wildlife like salmon and endangered Southern Resident orcas. It encourages community stewardship to help preserve the region’s ecosystems for future generations.

post-13561.title: Comment on Canada’s Trans Mountain Pipeline Expansion project by November 20th!
post-13561.summary: Friends asks islanders to comment to Canada's National Energy Board by November 20 against the Trans Mountain expansion, which would route tar sands tankers through Haro Strait and Boundary Pass. A Tsleil-Waututh study finds a 37 percent chance of a large tanker spill over fifty years, which could push Southern Resident orcas toward extinction.

The increased risk of diluted bitumen (dilbit) Alberta Tar Sands crude oil spills in our waters and the Southern Residents’ critical habitat is not justified […]

post-13563.title: Good News! Trans Mountain Pipeline Approval Rejected!
post-13563.summary: Canada's Federal Court of Appeal rejects approval of the Trans Mountain pipeline in August 2018 because the government ignored tanker traffic impacts on Southern Resident killer whales and failed to consult First Nations meaningfully. Construction halts, and Friends credits Salish Sea protectors who fought the project since 2013.

post-14000.title: Action Alert: Recent Salish Sea Salmon Spill
post-14000.summary: Up to 305,000 farmed Atlantic salmon escape when a Cooke Aquaculture net pen near Cypress Island breaks apart in 2017, threatening wild Pacific salmon with disease and competition. Friends asks islanders to thank the Governor for a permit moratorium and urge Ecology to block new net pens.

post-14000.excerpt: A major salmon spill in the Salish Sea released up to 305,000 Atlantic salmon after a fish farm near Cypress Island collapsed. Friends of the San Juans calls on the public to urge stronger protections against risky net-pen fish farming that can harm wild salmon and marine ecosystems.

Friends works to cut oil spill risk from tankers, over-water fuel transfers and fishing boats like the Aleutian Isle, which sank near San Juan Island in 2022.

page-14172.title: Our Core Values
page-14172.summary: Friends' five core values are reverence for interconnectedness, advocacy and justice, integrity, courage and steadfastness, and vigilant protection. page-12742.title: Green Boating

page-11637.title: The Future Through Education

page-11633.excerpt: Friends of the San Juans is a trusted and leading environmental nonprofit whose mission is to bring people and nature together to protect the San Juan Islands and the Salish Sea through education, science, policy, and law. Explore the heart of our work through people, stories, results, and collaboration.

page-11634.title: Get Involved
page-11634.summary: Friends offers several ways to get involved: volunteer on habitat projects, respond to action alerts on shoreline and clean water policy, attend events, or take the Green Boating pledge. Its Protector Priorities set science-based goals for the islands and the Salish Sea that guide community action.
